The Reproducibility and Negative Results (RENE) track of EASE 2027 invites rigorous empirical studies that investigate the robustness, transparency, validity, and generalisability of prior SE research. We welcome work that: Successfully reproduces or replicates previous findings Identifies and analyses barriers to reproducibility Demonstrates limitations or unexpected behaviour Reports well-founded negative, null, or surprising results The track is particularly interested in research that goes beyond simply confirming or failing to confirm previous findings. Submissions should provide useful explanations, methodological insights, or actionable recommendations that help researchers and practitioners understand when, why, and under what conditions empirical SE findings hold. This includes work examining the reproducibility and robustness of studies involving artificial intelligence and machine learning , including large language models (LLMs) and AI-based software engineering tools. Investigations of how changes in software ecosystems affect the long-term reproducibility of empirical studies. Studies concerning the reproducibility of secondary studies , including systematic literature reviews, systematic mapping studies, and multivocal literature reviews. 4. AI and Emerging Software Engineering Technologies Given the rapid growth of AI-based software engineering research, we particularly welcome reproducibility and negative-results studies involving: Large language models and code-generation models. AI-assisted software development tools and coding agents. Retrieval-augmented generation and tool-using AI systems. AI-based testing, debugging, program repair, code review, and software maintenance. Machine-learning-based software engineering techniques. Benchmark and dataset contamination or leakage. Effects of model version changes, prompting strategies, inference parameters, or nondeterminism. Comparisons between proprietary and open models. Evaluation Criteria Submissions to the RENE track will be evaluated according to the standards-based review approach used by EASE 2027, together with the following considerations. EASE 2027’s review criteria emphasise: Soundness Significance Novelty Verifiability and transparency Presentation Rigorousness and Soundness The study should employ appropriate and rigorous empirical methods. In particular, claims about failed reproduction, replication, or negative results should be supported by sufficiently thorough investigation and analysis. Significance and Usefulness The study should provide useful insights beyond the observation that a result could or could not be reproduced. Contributions may include: Explanations of discrepancies Identification of boundary conditions Methodological recommendations Evidence about generalisability Implications for researchers and practitioners Novelty The submission should provide an original contribution to knowledge about the robustness, validity, reproducibility, generalisability, or interpretation of empirical

ralisability, or interpretation of empirical SE findings. Verifiability and Transparency Authors should provide sufficient information and, where possible, research artifacts to allow others to understand, verify, reproduce, or extend the study. Relevant artifacts may include: Source code Datasets Analysis scripts Experimental configurations Documentation Replication packages Computational environments Other research materials Authors are strongly encouraged to use persistent repositories and provide complete, well-documented artifact packages. Appropriate Interpretation of Negative Results A negative or non-significant result should reflect an absence or reversal of an effect , rather than primarily reflecting inadequate methodology. For example, a paper is not a suitable RENE submission merely because: The sample is too small to provide meaningful statistical power. The study was poorly designed or executed. The experimental procedure was substantially different from the original without adequate justification. The authors stopped after encountering an easily repairable implementation problem. Studies investigating the reproducibility of computational and AI/ML-based SE research, including the effects of model versions, prompts, configurations, inference settings, nondeterminism, and proprietary or inaccessible models. Studies that evaluate whether published claims remain valid when the original study is conducted using independent implementations, alternative tools, or alternative analysis pipelines . Research examining the relationship between artifact availability, documentation quality, and successful reproduction or replication. Important: A paper whose sole contribution is that the authors successfully reran an existing study and obtained substantially the same results is generally not sufficient . Reproducibility studies should provide additional insight into the robustness, boundary conditions, explanations, or implications of the reproduced findings. Likewise, a failure to reproduce a result should be supported by systematic investigation. Authors should distinguish, where possible, between failures caused by inaccessible or incomplete artifacts and genuine differences in empirical outcomes. 2. Negative, Null, a

s in empirical SE. Key principle: Negative results should be informative rather than merely disappointing . The contribution should help narrow the space of plausible explanations, identify boundary conditions, expose methodological weaknesses, or provide guidance for future research and practice. 3. Reproducibility, Transparency, and Research Practice The track also welcomes studies that investigate broader methodological questions concerning the credibility and transparency of empirical SE research, including: Empirical assessments of research artifact availability and usability. Studies of replication packages, datasets, source code, experimental scripts, and computational environments. Analyses of the completeness and quality of empirical reporting. Studies of how documentation, artifact preservation, or open-science practices affect reproducibility. Empirical evaluations of reproducibility and replication standards.
